title: Federal Subsidies for Health Insurance, 2026 to 2036
key_claim: CBO and JCT project federal health-insurance subsidies of $33.6 trillion over 2026-2036, of which employment-based coverage accounts for $7.2 trillion (21%) and the premium tax credit and related spending only $1.2 trillion (4%); nearly 50% of the population is projected to hold employment-based coverage across the period, while the uninsured grow from 30 million in 2026 to 37 million in 2036.
frame_summary: Treats employment-based coverage as the durable centre of gravity in US health financing and projects the uninsured rising mainly because of the 2025 reconciliation act's cuts to Medicaid and CHIP, framing marketplace shrinkage as a secondary rather than primary driver.
verbatim_quote: An average of 318 million people are projected to have health insurance in any given month from 2026 to 2036; nearly 50 percent of the total population would be enrolled in employment-based coverage.
verbatim_list: Employment-based coverage—$7.2 trillion (21 percent),
The premium tax credit and related spending—$1.2 trillion (4 percent), and
The number of uninsured people in CBO's projections grows from 30 million in 2026 to 37 million in 2036

title: Exchange Coverage Remains Near Record High as 23.1 Million Enroll in 2026
date_evidence: Press Releases Mar 27, 2026 | dateline on CMS newsroom page
key_claim: During the 2026 Open Enrollment Period, 23.1 million consumers selected or were automatically re-enrolled in Exchange coverage; plan choices shifted sharply, with 40% choosing Bronze (up 10 percentage points on 2025), 43% Silver (down nearly 14 points) and 17% Gold (up 4 points).
frame_summary: Frames the individual market as structurally strong and stable despite subsidy withdrawal, presenting record plan selections and enforcement against improper enrolments as evidence of a well-functioning Exchange rather than a market under strain.
verbatim_quote: Plan choices shifted, with 40% of enrollees selecting Bronze plans, 43% Silver, and 17% Gold.
verbatim_list: During the 2026 Open Enrollment Period (OEP), 23.1 million consumers selected or were automatically re-enrolled in coverage through HealthCare.gov and State-Based Exchanges.
Compared to the 2025 OEP, Bronze plan enrollment increased by 10 percentage points, Gold increased by 4 points, and Silver decreased by nearly 14 points.
notes: Structural anchor (3-6 month band): the canonical federal statement of 2026 plan-selection composition, published 27/03/2026. CMS notes this release does not report effectuated enrolments, which is why the CBPP/CMS effectuation data is cited alongside it. title: ACA Marketplace Enrollment Shrank in Nearly Every State After Premium Tax Credit Enhancements Expired
key_claim: Analysing new CMS effectuated-enrolment data, CBPP finds US marketplace effectuated enrolment fell from 21,776,626 in February 2025 to 19,169,148 in February 2026, a decline of 2,607,478 people or 12%, with state-based marketplaces generally experiencing less severe losses than HealthCare.gov states.
frame_summary: Argues that the expiry of the enhanced premium tax credits, a political choice, caused a near-universal contraction in marketplace coverage, and that state-level mitigation explains why state-based marketplaces held up better.
verbatim_quote: Effectuated enrollment in the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplaces shrank in nearly every state after premium tax credit (PTC) enhancements expired,
verbatim_list: An accompanying report found that nationally, effectuated enrollment in the ACA marketplaces declined by nearly 3 million people between February 2025 and February 2026.
The new CMS data indicate that state-based marketplaces (SBMs) generally experienced less severe coverage losses than states using the federally facilitated marketplace, HealthCare.gov.

title: In Preliminary Rate Filings, ACA Marketplace Insurers Largely Propose Double-Digit Premium Increase For 2027
key_claim: ACA Marketplace insurers are proposing a median premium increase of 14% for 2027 across 77 insurers in 16 states and DC, a likely second consecutive year of double-digit rises; insurers estimate the sicker risk pool drove 2026 premiums up by roughly four percentage points and expect another four-point increase in 2027.
frame_summary: Argues that the individual market is entering a self-reinforcing deterioration, in which subsidy withdrawal drives healthier enrollees out, worsens the risk pool and pushes premiums up again, with regulatory changes compounding the effect.
verbatim_quote: Insurers estimate that the sicker risk pool drove 2026 premiums up by roughly four percentage points and expect another four percentage point increase in 2027.
verbatim_list: ACA Marketplace insurers are proposing a median premium increase of 14% for 2027— indicating a likely second consecutive year of double-digit increases, according to a new analysis of preliminary rate filings in 16 states and DC.
If these increases hold, typical premiums for insurers participating in the ACA Marketplaces would jump by more than one-third between 2025 and 2027.
This caused many healthier enrollees to leave the ACA Marketplaces in 2026, leaving behind a smaller number of enrollees who are somewhat sicker and more expensive to cover on average.
notes: Tier 2 health-policy research organisation. Figures are preliminary filings from 16 states and DC as of 08/07/2026; later KFF updates covering all 50 states report a higher median, so this scan cites the July filing analysis as published. title: Employers face 'existential reckoning' as health costs surge
key_claim: The Business Group on Health's 2027 survey of 127 employers covering some 8.7 million people finds a projected median 9.2% increase in health costs for 2027, cumulative growth of 76% over the decade, employers having underestimated actual spend for three consecutive years, and BGH's chief executive describing a growing existential reckoning about employers' role in healthcare.
frame_summary: Argues that employer health costs have become both unaffordable and unforecastable, and that this is forcing employers into a philosophical reappraisal of whether they can continue to serve as the backbone of the US insurance system.
verbatim_quote: Employers are projecting a median 9.2% increase in health costs in 2027, as hospital prices rise, drugs get more expensive and workers and their families simply get sicker, the Business Group on Health, a nonprofit that represents employers on health benefits issues, found in its latest survey.
verbatim_list: The BGH surveyed 127 employers covering some 8.7 million Americans for its research.
Factoring in predicted trend for 2026 and 2027, cumulative healthcare costs will have jumped 76% over the past decade — more than double the rate of general inflation, the BGH found.
But employers have underestimated actual medical spend for the past three years.
The percentage of employers covering GLP-1s in that category dropped from 72% last year to 60% this year, according to the survey.
notes: Specialist trade press reporting the Business Group on Health 2027 Employer Healthcare Strategy Survey. Quote and date confirmed by hand against the live page during the 30/08/2026 WebFetch sweep; sandbox audit fetch blocked (403 tunnel), so provenance is analyst-attested.

title: ICHRAs, a growth opportunity for insurers, face uphill battle
key_claim: Total ICHRA and QSEHRA adoption rose 19% from 2024 to 2025 with a 34% increase among large employers; fully insured large-group enrolment fell from about 46 million in 2013 to around 38 million in 2023 and small-group from about 17 million to roughly 10 million, while experts warn individual-market instability and rate rises erode the savings ICHRA offers.
frame_summary: Argues that ICHRAs are a genuine growth channel for insurers facing a stagnant commercial market but that their viability is hostage to the stability of the ACA individual market, and that they represent a shift of the payer's customer from employer to individual consumer.
verbatim_quote: Enrollment in fully insured plans in the large group market fell from approximately 46 million in 2013 to around 38 million in 2023, according to the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker.
verbatim_list: total ICHRA and QSEHRA adoption increased by 19% from 2024 to 2025, with a 34% increase among large employers.
Similarly, enrollment in fully insured plans in the small group market dropped from around 17 million in 2013 to roughly 10 million in 2023, according to the tracker.

“This is a major disruptor for the risk pool,” Anne Winter, senior managing director at FTI Consulting, said in an email. “Many states have seen huge rate increases, which lessens the value of the savings ICHRA brings.”

title: Strong ICHRA Growth Among Large Employers Strengthens ACA Marketplace and Risk Pool, HRA Council Report Finds
key_claim: Volume 5 of the HRA Council's annual report, aggregating data from 17 member organisations, says more than 20,000 US businesses offer ICHRA or QSEHRA in 2026 to at least 500,000 employees, that Applicable Large Employers are the fastest-growing segment and more than doubled on average since last year, and that more than half of enrolments are by employees under 45.
frame_summary: Advocates for ICHRA as a maturing, mainstream benefit that strengthens rather than destabilises the ACA risk pool by bringing in a younger cohort, and presses for statutory codification of arrangements currently created by regulation.
verbatim_quote: Applicable Large Employers (ALEs) represent the fastest growing segment of ICHRA adoption, more than doubling on average since last year.
verbatim_list: New research shows more than 20,000 US businesses offer ICHRA or QSEHRA as a health benefit in 2026 to at least 500,000 employees
The data suggests the number of ICHRA-covered lives alone (not including the thousands of QSEHRA-covered lives) surpassed 500,000 at the beginning of 2026.
More than half of enrollments both on- and off-exchange are by employees under the age of 45:
More than two-thirds of small businesses offering ICHRA and 93% of those newly offering QSEHRA in 2026 previously offered no health coverage to their employees.
